summary: AE+SE ran a POC scoping for Lyra Financial focused on workload characterization and traffic modeling. Discussed QPS, concurrency, input/output token distributions, latency SLOs, and benchmark methodology. Agreement to exchange traffic samples, run a two-week POC with dedicated capacity, and perform a controlled benchmark run. Outstanding: customer to share logs and security contacts; Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet and SOC2 docs.
transcript: [00:00] Jamie: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, i'll kick us off. this is jamie from redwood, ravi is our se. Sara: thanks, Jamie. we wanted to make sure we cover our production qps and expected latency targets. [00:28] Ravi: cool, can you walk me through current traffic patterns? qps, peak concurrency, typical payload sizes? Sara: yea so our APi sees 120 rps average, peaks around 600 for end-of-day batch and spikes to about 1.2k for promos; concurrency at peak roughly 80 concurrent inference threads but that's a bit fuzzy because some requests are short. [00:50] Derek: and most of our inference calls are for customer support summarization and policy checks, so inputs are variable, anywhere from 20 tokens to 1,200 tokens but median is about 180. output tends to be 40-250 tokens. [01:10] Jamie: ok good, that's already super helpful. quick note on terminology - when you say tokens are those BPE tokens or word counts? Sara: it's tokenizer tokens, we use tiktoken-ish counts. [01:26] Ravi: perfect. a couple of things we'll look at for the poc: qps/concurrency mapping to GPU capacity, latency p95/p99 targets, and cost per 1k tokens. also we typically recommend collecting a representative sample of 1-2 weeks of requests so we can model distribution. [01:46] Alejandra: we can export the logs, but note some fields are scrubbed for pii. is that ok? Derek: also security is a concern - we need to understand vpc/on-prem options. [02:05] Jamie: absolutely. for the poc we support three deployment modes: hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, and private vpc/on-prem. for initial benchmarking, dedicated is usually simplest to get consistent numbers. [02:22] Sara: curious about latency targets - our business needs p95 < 450 ms for short chat-like requests, and for the long summaries p95 < 2s is acceptable. is that realistic? [02:38] Ravi: with dedicated capacity and a model in the 7-13B family, that's achievable for short requests, assuming batching config is tuned. clearly longer inputs will increase latencies. [02:52] Speaker 2: are you guys using kv cache? i heard something about caching prefixes. [02:58] Ravi: yes we do prefix and KV cache, helps a lot for repeated contexts. side note we sometimes see transcripts where 'kv cache' transcribed as 'KV cash' so ignore that in export. [03:14] Tom: the malformed transcription is hilarious. [03:18] Jamie: so to model your workload we'll need: real qps distribution (per-minute), token histograms for input/output, percent of requests that can be cached, and latency SLO per request class. [03:33] Sara: we can do that - we'll pull sample logs and a small synthetic set for very long inputs. [03:40] Ravi: great. on benchmarking approach: we propose three stages - 1) offline modeling from logs to estimate GPU needs and qps mapping, 2) controlled benchmark on dedicated GPU pools to validate p95/p99 and throughput, 3) short production pilot with real traffic and monitoring for 2 weeks. [04:01] Derek: sounds reasonable. what about quantization and model choice? we need good accuracy on policy checks so can't degrade quality. [04:12] Ravi: understood. we'll recommend a model family and quantization profile and run quality checks against your eval set; if redwood verify shows regression beyond your threshold we'll fallback to higher precision. [04:24] Sara: what are typical qps-to-gpu numbers? like one a100 can do how much for 7b vs 13b? [04:33] Ravi: give or take, for synchronous low-latency 7B with 256 max tokens you might see 60-120 qps per GPU depending on batching and kernel tuning; 13B drops to 20-40 qps. these are rough but helpful starting points. [04:52] Jamie: also important is concurrency - if you need 80 concurrent sessions with low-latency, you might want multiple smaller instances instead of a single large queued pool. [05:04] Alejandra: can you explain how batching affects latency vs cost? i.e., we want to save on tokens but not blow p95. [05:13] Ravi: batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token but increases per-request latency depending on batching window. Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching and latency-aware thresholds so you can set a p95 cap and it will avoid excessive batch delays. [05:30] Speaker 2: can we see the real benchmark tools? [05:34] Jamie: yes we'll share the benchmark harness and a spreadsheet. our benchmark harness will replay logs at configurable qps and token distributions, and measure p50/p95/p99 and cost. [05:46] Tom: on reporting, we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency. [05:50] Ravi: that's in the console - trace ids, per-request token counts, and KV cache hit rates. [06:00] Sara: ok next, success criteria - what should we set for this poc? Derek: for us, success is: meet p95 targets for the three request classes, maintain accuracy within 1-2% of our baseline eval set, and demonstrate predictable monthly unit costs. [06:19] Jamie: nice and measurable. we'll draft a success criteria doc: performance (p95 targets), quality (eval pass rate), cost predictability (cost per 1M tokens within agreed range). [06:30] Ravi: timeline wise: if you can drop logs by Friday (2026-11-06), we can run offline modeling over the following week, share an initial GPU sizing and benchmark plan by 2026-11-12, and schedule the controlled run week of 2026-11-16. does that align? [06:48] Sara: yes that works for us. [06:51] Alejandra: small ops question: for dedicated, how long to provision GPUs? can you do short bursts? [06:58] Jamie: typical provisioning is 3-5 business days for Dedicated pools; we can provision short burst capacity for a benchmark but reserved capacity gives predictable throughput. [07:09] Ravi: also remember autoscaling policies - you can configure headroom and burst rules for traffic spikes. [07:18] Tom: do we need to white-list IPs for VPC peering? Alejandra: yes we have a strict firewall. [07:24] Jamie: we'll coordinate with your infra team; we'll send a checklist. [07:28] Derek: security - can you share SOC2 + encryption at rest details? [07:33] Jamie: yes, we'll attach SOC2, ISO summary and KMS integration docs. we'll also include audit log formats. [07:41] Sara: on modeling, are you going to simulate cache hit rates? some of our traffic is highly repetitive. [07:47] Ravi: yes we model cacheable prefixes and show sensitivity analysis - if cache hit drops from 60% to 20% your GPU needs scale accordingly. we'll include charts in the spreadsheet. [07:58] Speaker 2: any thoughts on embeddings/semantic search calls - those are separate flow but similar considerations? [08:04] Ravi: separate flow, different models and cost profile; we'll capture that but focus POC on generation and policy checks first. [08:12] Jamie: ok, to recap quick: Lyra to send logs + eval set; Redwood to share benchmark harness, SOW template, security docs, and proposed sizing by 11/12. controlled run tentatively 11/16. [08:30] Sara: yep, and we'll confirm infra contacts. [08:35] Alejandra: action - i'll open a ticket for the peering window. [08:38] Jamie: perfect. any last questions? [08:41] Derek: one on metrics - you'll measure cost per 1M tokens including caching? [08:46] Ravi: yes cost will be token-billed and we'll show effective token cost after caching/aggregation.
notes: References: benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat), SOC2 package, POC SOW template. Mentioned model families (7B, 13B) and KV cache; occasional transcription errors (e.g., 'KV cash') in auto transcript.
